core: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rock formation
weathering, erosion, deposition, lithification, metamorphism, melting, and cooling
multiple pathways in the rock cycle

claims.claim: The rock cycle has no single starting point and includes many pathways through which igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks can change.

Igneous rocks form when magma or lava cools and solidifies, sedimentary rocks form from sediment through processes including compaction and cementation, and metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are altered by heat and pressure.
Weathering breaks down or chemically alters rock at or near the surface, while erosion moves weathered material from one location to another.
Mechanical weathering breaks rock into fragments without changing the chemical makeup of the individual minerals, whereas chemical weathering changes at least some minerals.
Deposition is accumulation of transported material, and loose sediment requires lithification processes such as compaction and cementation to become sedimentary rock.
Metamorphism changes rock while it remains solid; melting produces magma, which can cool and solidify into igneous rock.
Plate tectonics helps drive pressure and melting that recycle material into metamorphic and igneous rocks, while weathering and erosion connect rocks to surface sediment pathways.
